subtype: Approach: putting all text on slides and reading it out [Pitfall]
passage: In the seminar hall on the second floor, Rafiq stood at the lectern as the projector warmed up. Every slide was full: whole paragraphs in small type, copied from the report because Rafiq was afraid of losing the thread. Rafiq began to read from the screen, word for word, with eyes turned to the wall. By slide three the audience had already read ahead. Nikita, in the second row, stopped taking notes. A lecturer glanced at the wristwatch. Someone yawned. A student asked a question about a point three slides back, since nobody could recall what had been said. Rafiq finished four minutes early and looked at the floor. The clapping was polite and short.

qa.q: Where did Rafiq stand when the projector warmed up?
qa.a: Rafiq stood at the lectern in the seminar hall on the second floor.

qa.q: What was Rafiq afraid of when filling the slides with paragraphs?
qa.a: Rafiq was afraid of forgetting what to say and losing the thread, so the report text went onto every slide.

qa.q: What could Rafiq try next time instead of reading the slides, and why?
qa.a: Rafiq could keep a few words on each slide and practise saying the rest, because the audience listens to a speaker but reads faster than anyone can talk.

qa.q: How did Nikita and the audience experience the talk?
qa.a: Nikita and others read ahead, lost interest and stopped taking notes, so nobody remembered what had been said.

grounding: A student fills slides with paragraphs out of fear and reads them aloud, and the audience loses interest.

subtype: Approach: putting all text on slides and reading it out [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Lakshmi,
You asked how my big presentation went. Honestly? Badly, and I know why.
I was so scared of forgetting something that I wrote everything on the slides. Full paragraphs. Some slides had eight bullet points of two lines each. My plan was simple: if my mind went blank, I'd just read.
My mind didn't go blank. I read anyway, because it was there. About three slides in, I saw the professor had already finished the slide and was looking at her phone. Two students in the front row were whispering. They could read faster than I could talk, so there was nothing left for me to add.
The worst moment was the end, when she asked a question and I realised I'd been reading so hard I had barely thought about what I was saying.
Next time: fewer words, more pictures, and notes on a card only I can see.
Sabina

qa.q: How many bullet points did some slides have?
qa.a: Eight bullet points of two lines each.

qa.q: Why did Sabina fill the slides with paragraphs, and how did it feel in the room?
qa.a: Sabina was scared of forgetting, and in the room felt embarrassed and deflated watching the audience lose interest.

qa.q: What could Sabina change first for the next presentation?
qa.a: Keep only a few words or a picture on each slide and put the full points on a card, so the audience listens instead of reading.

qa.q: How might the professor have experienced the talk?
qa.a: The professor finished each slide before Sabina did, grew bored and turned to the phone.

grounding: Shows a student who, afraid of forgetting, fills slides with paragraphs and reads them, so the audience reads ahead and loses interest.

subtype: Approach: putting all text on slides and reading it out [Pitfall]
passage:
Mehak, before you make your slides, let me, Rafiq, confess the worst fifteen minutes of my college life.
The departmental seminar, third year. I was terrified of freezing, so I typed my whole speech onto the slides. Every word. White background, small black text, twenty slides.
I stood there and read. Slide one. Slide two. By slide four I could hear chairs creaking. People had already read ahead and were waiting for me to catch up. Someone at the back yawned so loudly the class laughed. I didn't look up once, because if I looked up I'd lose my place in the paragraph.
Afterwards my friend said, 'Why did you even come? We could've just read the file.' He was joking, but he was right.
So please: a few words on the slide, the rest in your head or on a card. They came to hear you.

qa.q: How many slides did Rafiq have?
Why didn't Rafiq look up during the talk, and what does that show about how Rafiq felt?
qa.a: Rafiq was afraid of losing the place in the paragraph, which shows how anxious and dependent on the text Rafiq was.

qa.q: What would you advise Mehak to prepare instead of full-text slides?
qa.a: Short slides with a few words or a picture, plus a card of key points to glance at if needed.

qa.q: How did the audience experience the seminar?
qa.a: They read ahead, grew bored and restless, and one friend joked that they could have just read the file.

grounding: Shows a student who puts a whole speech on slides and reads it, so the audience reads ahead and loses interest.
